catalog_quote: Rules (unamended version): I. Mark X^n. II. (a) Mark every primary syllable; (b) mark every 2° bordered by at least one syllable weaker than itself. (Consider X^n to be no weaker than X^(n-1). Consider (preceding) open juncture to be weaker than X1.) (c) Mark every weak (3°, 4°) syllable preceding a syllable weaker than itself. ... III. Each supra-minimal USS must be reduced to minimal stretches by marking one or more of its syllables. Mark the first syllable of an initial supra-minimal USS and every odd-numbered syllable following it until no supra-minimal USS remains; mark the second syllable of a homogeneous medial supra-minimal USS and every odd-numbered syllable following it until no non-minimal USS remains ... Amendments: I. Mark every X^n unless that X^n be a lengthening or a diphthongisation, in which case mark X^(n-1). IV. Stress the initial syllable of any PW whose final syllable is not lengthening or diphthongisation (i.e. whose final syllable is stressed) which has only one stress. Examples: (1.) /kokosomoroden/; by I <-----+>; by IIa <+---++>; by III <+-+-++.>. ... (2.) /kokoyoba/; by I <---+>; by II <+--+.>. (3.) /mudakekukiba/; by I <-----+>; by II <-+---+>; by III <-+-+-+.>. (4.) /gada/; by I <-+>; by IV <++.>. The syllable types and syllable formulae for these are: (1) CV^ccVCVCVCVCVC, S-z-Z-Z-S-s, 1-4-3-3-1-1; (2) CV^ccVYVCV, S-z-Y-Z, 1-4-4-3; (3) CVCVCVCVCVCV, Z-Z-Z-Z-Z-Z, 3-2-3-3-3-3; (4) CVCV, Z-Z, 3-3.

sweep_summary: Korku (kork1243) is not in the catalog. The single title hit, Zide 1979 'Korku Syllables and Syllable Stress' (Pacific Linguistics C-45: 161-186), is open access on ANU Open Research (hdl 1885/144545, CC BY-SA); sealang.net and web.archive.org were could not be reached by automated download, and the archive.org scan is lending-only, so the ANU PDF was downloaded (whole volume + chapter split, text, page scan) and fully read. It is a first-hand, complete rule system reproduced unaltered from Zide's 1960 U. Penn. dissertation (fieldwork 1956-8, Dharni dialect): final syllable always stressed (penult instead when the final is a lengthening/diphthongisation), closed syllables stressed beside weaker open ones, alternating stress across unstressed stretches, initial stress added when a word has only one stress (disyllables <++>), with residual phonemic stress shown to be morphophonemically predictable. It confirms and greatly refines the on-disk Zide 2008: 260 snippet summary ('largely automatic, determined by syllable weight.. and position, final position syllables having more weight than initial ones') and should be the deciding source if Korku is added: weight-sensitive, right-edge anchored, multiple/rhythmic stress. Not read: Zide 1960 dissertation (low priority, since 1979 reprints its stress sections) and the full pages 6-7 of Drake 1903 (Google Books full view; 'accent is irregular'; medium priority as the only pre-Zide statement).

new_statements.quote: 2.5 Intonation/stress. Stress is largely automatic, determined by the syllable weight (closed syllables, those with final consonant, are heavier than open syllables) and position, final position syllables having more weight than initial ones. The earlier mention of longer[,] that is, half-long or longer than simple single stops, but less longer than geminate stops (for example, ti(tt)ipi above), can be considered to reflect phonemically stressed initial syllables. Initial syllables of reduplicated verb forms perhaps generally get more (not necessarily phonemically) stressed, but they are - phonemically - stressed where the syllable weight would not otherwise give them the requisite stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is mostly predictable from weight and position: closed (CVC) syllables are heavier than open ones and final syllables outweigh initial ones, so in a disyllable the final syllable is stressed unless only the initial is heavy (right-oriented, quantity-sensitive). A residue of phonemic (unpredictable) initial stress exists, signalled by half-long following stops (ti(tt)ipi) and found on initial syllables of reduplicated verb forms.
new_statements.exceptions: Phonemically stressed initial syllables (reflected in half-long medial stops, e.g. ti(tt)ipi); initial syllables of reduplicated verb forms are phonemically stressed where weight would not assign them stress; medial CV syllables are short/reduced (kath(ə)làʔ 'armpit'), which Nagaraja treats as zero vowels. Korku also has a low-tone contrast on non-initial syllables (Zide 1966), independent of stress. Hildebrandt & Anderson 2023: 558-559 restate the rule as 'quantity sensitive with a right-headed orientation' but warn 'very little confidence.. can be assigned to these interpretations'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on Zide's disyllable-oriented description (Dharni/Amraoti and Lahi/Hoshangabad dialects, fieldwork 1956-63); intonation explicitly left for future research. Text recovered from overlapping Google Books snippets, not a page scan; one short gap before the final sentence of the section.
new_statements.identity_note: Zide's description rests on Dharni (Amravati dist., Maharashtra) Korku with comparison to Lahi (Hoshangabad, MP) Korku (Zide 1966: 216 fn. 1; 1960 diss. record 'Korku as spoken in Amraoti District'); both fall under kork1243 (no separate Glottolog dialect codes used here).

new_statements.reading: Korku (Dharni dialect) word stress is rule-governed, weight-sensitive and multiple: within a phonological word (stem plus suffixes/enclitics) the final syllable is always stressed (X^n = last syllable; if it merely lengthens or diphthongises the penult, the penult is stressed instead); closed syllables (CVC, VC = 2° strength) are stressed when next to a weaker open syllable; runs of unstressed syllables are broken by alternating stress; and a word that would have only one stress also stresses its initial syllable, so plain CVCV disyllables are stressed on both syllables (/gada/ 'river' <++>). Worked examples: /kokoyoba/ <+--+>, /mudakekukiba/ <-+-+-+>, /kokosomoroden/ <+-+-++>. Residual cases carry phonemic stress that Zide shows is predictable from morpheme boundaries (verb-stem-final syllable before past {-eq}; CVC person-suffix syllables before {-keq}/{-den}/{-ba}; reduplicant initials). For catalog purposes: weight-sensitive, right-edge (final) anchored, with rhythmic alternation leftwards and initial reinforcement; no single culminative primary is identified. This is the full system that Zide 2008: 260 compresses to 'largely automatic, determined by syllable weight.. and position, final position syllables having more weight than initial ones', and it is the source Hildebrandt & Anderson 2023 (sec. 17.3.11) paraphrase second-hand.

tone.quote: Suprasegmental Features The suprasegmental phonemes are those phonemes in the language, which do not occur by themselves rather these are superimposed upon segmental phonemes. Following are the suprasegmental features available in Korku language. (i) Nasalization: / ͂ /- In Korku, all vowels are seen in nasalized forms, but /ə͂/ is not so productive. ... (ii) Junctures There are four kinds of junctures in Korku namely Syllabic Juncture marked by /./, word juncture by /-/,phrase juncture by / / and sentence juncture by /#/.
